papers.title: Short-term perioperative safety and long-term follow-up after robotic-assisted resection of non-renal, non-adrenal retroperitoneal tumors: a 10-year retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Open surgery remains the conventional approach for large retroperitoneal tumors because of limited operative space, complex vascular anatomy, potential bleeding risk, and oncological concerns. However, evidence regarding robotic-assisted laparoscopic resection for retroperitoneal tumors larger than 10 cm remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility, safety, perioperative outcomes, and follow-up results of robotic-assisted laparoscopic resection for non-renal and non-adrenal retroperitoneal tumors, with particular focus on tumors larger than 10 cm. We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent robotic-assisted laparoscopic resection of retroperitoneal tumors at our institution between November 2015 and November 2024. Tumors of renal or adrenal origin were excluded based on postoperative pathological diagnosis. Patients were stratified according to maximum tumor diameter into three groups: >10, >6 to <10, and <6 cm. Baseline characteristics, operative variables, perioperative outcomes, pathological findings, and follow-up results were compared among the three groups. The primary descriptive endpoints were conversion, estimated blood loss, transfusion, postoperative intensive care unit admission, operative time, and postoperative hospital stay. Comparisons were exploratory and unadjusted. A total of 207 patients were included, comprising 27 patients in the >10 cm group, 52 in the >6 to <10 cm group, and 128 in the <6 cm group. There were no significant differences among the groups in age, body mass index, sex distribution, American Society of Anesthesiologists grade, transfusion rate, conversion rate, postoperative intensive care unit admission, or follow-up duration. Two procedures (1.0%) were converted to open surgery. After inclusion of the 3,000 mL bleeding conversion, mean blood loss in the >10 cm group was 300.42±658.94 mL (F=6.4952, P=0.002). Operative time and postoperative hospital stay were longer in the >10 cm group. Malignancy was more frequent in tumors larger than 6 cm than in tumors smaller than 6 cm. In the >10 cm group, liposarcoma, ganglioneuroma, and paraganglioma were the most common pathological diagnoses. In the liposarcoma-specific review, 14 patients underwent 18 robotic procedures; six developed local recurrence, and one died of metastatic disease during follow-up. Robotic-assisted laparoscopic resection was technically feasible in this selected cohort for selected non-renal and non-adrenal retroperitoneal tumors larger than 10 cm when performed in experienced centers. Although larger tumors were associated with longer operative time and postoperative hospital stay, conversion and transfusion rates were low, one major bleeding conversion illustrates an important limitation. For large benign tumors, perioperative outcomes were broadly comparable with those of smaller tumors. For large malignant tumors, robotic surgery may represent a minimally invasive option with acceptable perioperative outcomes; however, careful patient selection and long-term oncological surveillance remain essential. These findings do not establish oncological equivalence to open surgery, particularly for retroperitoneal sarcoma.

papers.title: MRI-Guided Assessment of Rapid Locoregional Progression of Merkel Cell Carcinoma of the Thigh Following Wide Local Excision: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is a rare and highly aggressive neuroendocrine skin cancer with a marked predilection for elderly and immunosuppressed patients. Although most commonly cutaneous, MCC can present with extensive locoregional soft tissue involvement, and its clinical course is characterized by rapid growth, frequent local recurrence, and early lymphatic and distant spread. We report the case of a 74-year-old woman who underwent wide local excision of a solitary thigh mass, with histopathology confirming MCC and a lateral margin that was uninvolved but immeasurably close. The patient was lost to follow-up shortly after surgery and, as a result, did not receive the recommended adjuvant treatment. She presented three months later with progressive swelling of the limb. Follow-up magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed extensive, confluent cutaneous and subcutaneous masses spanning 32 cm along the thigh, infiltrating the adjacent muscular compartments, encasing the common femoral and common iliac vessels, and extending into the pelvis with intimate contact with the bladder wall and pelvic bones, without evidence of bone lysis. This dramatic progression, within only three months and in the absence of adjuvant therapy, rendered the lesion surgically unresectable. This case illustrates the aggressive natural history of MCC in an elderly patient lost to follow-up, highlights the central role of MRI in characterizing locoregional extension and supporting the assessment of surgical unresectability, and underscores the importance of adjuvant radiotherapy following excisions with close margins to prevent such outcomes.

papers.title: Synchronous medullary and papillary thyroid carcinoma with mixed-component lateral cervical lymph node metastases: a case report.
papers.abstract: Synchronous medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) and papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) are uncommon thyroid malignancies, whereas mixed-component cervical lymph node metastases containing both tumor components within the same metastatic deposit are exceptionally rare. This case highlights the diagnostic value of integrating discordant site-specific fine-needle aspiration (FNA) findings with serum biomarkers for preoperative recognition of this unusual presentation. A 65-year-old man presented with a progressively enlarging right-sided neck mass accompanied by ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy for more than two months. Ultrasonography demonstrated a 4.28 cm × 2.28 cm × 2.54 cm Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS) 5 thyroid nodule with multiple enlarged right cervical lymph nodes. Serum calcitonin (Ctn) (1,796.38 ng/L), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) (81.69 μg/L), and thyroglobulin (Tg) (163.65 μg/L) levels were markedly elevated. FNA of the thyroid nodule supported MTC, whereas FNA of a metastatic cervical lymph node demonstrated PTC, providing discordant cytological evidence that raised preoperative suspicion of synchronous thyroid malignancies. Total thyroidectomy with bilateral neck dissection revealed multifocal MTC and microscopic contralateral PTC with mixed-component metastases involving 10 cervical lymph nodes. No postoperative complications such as recurrent laryngeal nerve injury or permanent hypoparathyroidism occurred. Serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels recovered to 40.85 ng/L at 12 months. Serum Ctn, CEA, and Tg levels remained persistently low (57.29 ng/L, 3.96 μg/L, and 0.39 μg/L, respectively), and follow-up neck CT scans over the 12 months showed no signs of lymphadenopathy. This case demonstrates that discordant FNA results between primary thyroid lesions and metastatic lymph nodes, accompanied by dual-marker elevation (Ctn, CEA and Tg), strongly indicate synchronous MTC and PTC. A comprehensive radical surgical approach and rigorous dual-biomarker longitudinal surveillance are key to achieving optimal oncological control and preventing diagnostic omissions.

papers.title: Left ventricular thrombus formation in paraganglioma: a rare but serious complication - a case report.
papers.abstract: The incidence rate of paraganglioma stands at approximately 1 case per 300 000 person-years. Symptoms resembling anxiety and panic attacks are prevalent within the general populace, rendering the identification of individuals afflicted with pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma a formidable task for healthcare practitioners. A 43-year-old presented with ischemic signs that turned into necrosis at his left foot due to diffused thrombosis in his main arteries, furthermore Echodiagram indicated the presence of left ventricular thrombosis, through which the diagnosis of paraganglioma was made and confirmed through histological examination. Paragangliomas are rare tumors originating from extra-adrenal chromaffin cells, typically found in areas such as the carotid body and aortic arch. These tumors can cause cardiovascular issues like hypertension, tachycardia, and thrombus formation. In this case, a paraganglioma was detected below the renal arteries, an uncommon location, with extensive arterial and left ventricular thrombi. Paragangliomas induce a hypercoagulable state due to catecholamine excess, vasospasm, and vascular compression, as seen in this patient, who had thrombi in the lower extremities and aortic artery, increasing embolization risks. Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation, biochemical testing, and imaging studies, with surgical resection as the primary treatment. Preoperative management focuses on controlling blood pressure and glucose, while postoperative care includes anticoagulation therapy. This case highlights the multifaceted vascular complications of paragangliomas, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive diagnostic and treatment approach. Increasing follow-up sessions with this patient to prevent recurring issues, including the consideration of coronary vascular imaging and administrating anti-coagulant drugs.

papers.title: Medullary thyroid carcinoma with pheochromocytoma and cystic parathyroid degeneration in a ret-negative patient: a case report.
papers.abstract: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN2A) is a rare autosomal dominant hereditary cancer syndrome, predominantly caused by mutations of the RET proto-oncogene on chromosome 10q11.2. It typically presents with medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism. Cases with a MEN2A phenotype but negative RET testing are uncommon, posing challenges for diagnosis and patient management. We report the case of a 63-year-old female who was diagnosed with MTC and pheochromocytoma. and cystic parathyroid gland. Genetic workup was negative for RET proto-oncogene mutations but positive for a heterozygous variant in the TMEM127 tumor suppressor gene. MEN2A is associated with pathogenic germline variants in the RET proto-oncogene in approximately 95-99% of cases. Our patient, however, exhibited a MEN2A-like clinical phenotype in the absence of an identifiable RET mutation, with a pathogenic TMEM127 variant instead. Although TMEM127 is an established susceptibility gene for pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, its association with the broader MEN2A phenotype remains unclear. This unusual genotype-phenotype discordance raises important questions regarding the potential role of alternative genetic pathways in MEN2-like syndromes and creates uncertainty regarding postoperative surveillance and the appropriate extent of screening and genetic counseling for family members. Our case represents an unusual scenario where the patient presents with a clinical phenotype of MEN2A but is RET negative and positive heterozygous for a variant in the TMEM127. This atypical genetic finding introduces complexities in determining the appropriate follow-up protocol and the scope of familial screening necessary.

papers.title: Catecholamine-Secreting Retroperitoneal Paraganglioma: A Case Report and Literature Review.
papers.abstract: Paragangliomas are rare neuroendocrine tumors arising from autonomic paraganglia. These tumors have metastatic potential, and histopathological findings alone cannot reliably predict their biological behavior. Clinical manifestations range from the classic triad of headache, diaphoresis, and palpitations to incidental findings in asymptomatic patients. A 75-year-old man was incidentally found to have a 5 cm retroperitoneal mass adjacent to the right renal hilum. Biochemical testing confirmed marked catecholamine hypersecretion, and 18F-FDOPA PET/CT demonstrated isolated uptake within the lesion without additional disease. Preoperative preparation included progressive alpha-adrenergic blockade with doxazosin for approximately 1 month, followed by atenolol for heart rate control. An open approach through a right subcostal hemichevron incision was selected because the tumor was located between the right renal artery and vein and lateral to the inferior vena cava. During dissection, an iatrogenic renal artery injury with intraoperative hemorrhage occurred, necessitating en bloc removal of the tumor, right kidney, and right adrenal gland. Histopathological examination confirmed a paraganglioma with a Ki-67 proliferation index below 1%, focal nuclear atypia, no mitotic figures, no tumor necrosis, no vascular invasion, and microscopic margin involvement. Immunohistochemistry was positive for Chromogranin A, synaptophysin, GATA-3, and S100. Germline testing using a 14-gene pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma panel identified no reported pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants. At 6 months, contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominopelvic computed tomography showed no evidence of local recurrence or metastatic disease, and plasma and urinary metanephrines had normalized, consistent with postoperative biochemical remission. The patient remains under joint endocrinology and urology follow-up with lifelong annual clinical and biochemical surveillance. This case highlights the diagnostic and surgical challenges of a functioning perihilar retroperitoneal paraganglioma. Careful endocrine preparation, vascular planning, multidisciplinary management, and lifelong surveillance are essential, particularly when the surgical margin is microscopically involved.

papers.title: Lactate metabolism and lactylation in uveal melanoma: from metabolic adaptation to immune regulation.
papers.abstract: Uveal melanoma (UM) is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults. The liver is its most common site of metastasis, and in some patients, distant metastases may become clinically apparent years after treatment of the primary tumor. Metastatic UM generally shows limited responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade. Although genetic alterations in GNAQ, GNA11, BAP1, SF3B1, and EIF1AX are important for the molecular classification and prognostic stratification of UM, these factors do not fully explain late metastatic recurrence, persistence of low-proliferative tumor cell states, immune escape, or adaptation to the hepatic metastatic microenvironment. Lactate is not only a major product of glycolysis but also an immunometabolic regulator. Through monocarboxylate transporter-mediated transport, HCAR1/GPR81 signaling, extracellular vesicle-associated transfer, and lysine lactylation, lactate influences tumor cell states, tumor-immune metabolic communication, chromatin regulation, and post-transcriptional control. In UM cell studies, exogenous lactate induces a quiescence-like phenotype characterized by reduced proliferation and migration, increased oxidative metabolism, changes in chromatin organization, and elevated H3K18la levels. Tumor-derived lactate increases the stability of PD-L1 and HLA-E proteins through GPR81-related signaling, enhancing the resistance of UM cells to T cell- and NK cell-mediated killing. Under hypoxic conditions, extracellular vesicle-associated lactate participates in metabolic communication between tumor cells and immune cells, alters macrophage states, and impairs CD8+ T-cell effector function. Lactylation further links lactate metabolism with chromatin regulation and RNA modification-related post-transcriptional control. Studies in related ocular melanoma models indicate that H3K18la regulates YTHDF2 and ALKBH3 and thereby affects m6A- and m¹A-associated RNA regulation. This review summarizes current studies on lactate production, transport, receptor signaling, extracellular vesicle-associated lactate transfer, and lactylation in UM and related ocular melanoma models, and discusses their roles in low-proliferative adaptation, tumor-immune metabolic communication, hepatic metastatic microenvironment adaptation, and therapeutic resistance.

papers.title: Case Report: Apparent progressive complete mismatch repair protein loss during platinum-based chemotherapy in metastatic rectal neuroendocrine tumour grade 2.
papers.abstract: Mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency is uncommon in gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (GEP-NETs), yet it represents a critical biomarker for immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) eligibility. Treatment-associated reduction or loss of MMR protein expression, often without corresponding MSI-H, has been reported in colorectal adenocarcinoma, but comparable changes have not been described in neuroendocrine tumours. Persistent discordance between immunohistochemistry (IHC)-based MMR protein assessment and next-generation sequencing (NGS)-based microsatellite instability (MSI) testing is an emerging and clinically challenging phenomenon. We report a 55-year-old woman initially diagnosed with rectal NET Grade 1 on endoscopic biopsy; the tumour was upgraded to NET Grade 2 (Ki-67 approximately 20%) on the surgical resectionk specimen. Hepatic metastases were confirmed four months after resection. The first liver biopsy (January 16, 2026) demonstrated partial MMR protein loss by IHC (MLH1-, MSH2+, MSH6-, PMS2-), while concurrent NGS showed microsatellite stability (MSS) and a tumour mutational burden (TMB) of <1 mut/Mb. The patient received two cycles of surufatinib 250 mg orally once daily combined with intravenous carboplatin (500 mg, day 1) and etoposide (160 mg, days 1-3). Restaging CT demonstrated disease progression. A repeat liver biopsy (March 17, 2026) revealed complete loss of all four MMR proteins by IHC (MLH1-, MSH2-, MSH6-, PMS2-), while NGS again confirmed MSS and TMB <1 mut/Mb. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reported case of apparent progressive complete MMR protein loss in the context of sequential platinum-based chemotherapy in metastatic rectal NET Grade 2, with persistent IHC-NGS discordance throughout. These findings raise an important question regarding how IHC-defined dMMR should be interpreted in the absence of NGS-confirmed MSI-H, and highlight the complexity of immunotherapy eligibility decisions in rare tumour types. Prospective data are needed to guide clinical practice.

papers.title: Unmet needs and associated factors among patients with melanoma: a mixed-methods study.
papers.abstract: The burden of melanoma in China is increasing, but the supportive care needs of Chinese patients remain understudied. The applicability of Western findings may be limited by clinical and sociocultural differences. This study aimed to characterize unmet needs among Chinese patients with melanoma and identify associated factors using a mixed-methods approach. A convergent parallel mixed-methods study was conducted. Quantitatively, 105 patients completed the Needs Evaluation Questionnaire, and multivariable binary logistic regression was performed to identify associated factors. Qualitatively, semi-structured interviews were conducted with an independent sample of 16 patients. Directed content analysis was guided by the Social Ecological Model. The quantitative and qualitative findings were integrated through a joint analysis. Information needs were the most frequently reported unmet needs. In the multivariable model, female patients had lower odds of high unmet needs than male patients (OR = 0.257, 95%CI: 0.080-0.830, p = 0.023). Internet-based health information use was also associated with lower odds of high unmet needs (OR = 0.075, 95%CI: 0.022-0.257, p < 0.001). Nine qualitative themes were identified across individual, family/community, and sociocultural levels. Individual-level factors were most prominent. The integrated findings reflected the interplay of personal vulnerability, social support, healthcare access, information resources, and sociocultural contexts. Unmet needs, particularly information needs, were prominent among Chinese patients with melanoma and reflected factors across multiple ecological levels. Patient-centered care should prioritize tailored information support and address barriers to healthcare access and supportive resources.

papers.title: Single-cell transcriptomics reveals transcriptional reprogramming and microenvironmental remodeling in ectopic ACTH/CRH-secreting pheochromocytomas.
papers.abstract: Ectopic ACTH- and/or CRH-secreting pheochromocytomas (ACTH+CRH+PCCs) are rare tumors that can mimic Cushing's syndrome and complicate the diagnosis and treatment clinically. However, the tumor-intrinsic and microenvironmental features of ACTH+CRH+ PCCs remains poorly understood. Fresh tumor specimens from three ACTH+CRH+ and three ACTH- CRH- PCCs were profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing. Developmental trajectories and transcriptional regulatory networks were analyzed to investigate tumor-intrinsic programs, while CellChat and NicheNet were used to characterize cell-cell communication and infer ligand-mediated microenvironmental remodeling. Findings were also validated using TCGA datasets and immunohistochemical staining. ACTH+ CRH+ PCCs showed increased POMC and CRH expression and were enriched for a Schwann cell precursor (SCP)-like population positioned at an early pseudotime state. Regulatory network analysis further identified increased CEBPB activity in ACTH+ CRH+ tumor cells. Microenvironmental analysis revealed enrichment of SELE+ endothelial cells and CD8+ T cells in ACTH+ CRH+ PCCs. Cell-cell communication analysis showed more frequent interactions between ACTH+ CRH+ tumor cells and SELE+ endothelial cells, together with predicted ECM-associated interactions between SELE+ endothelial cells and T cells. In contrast, ACTH- CRH- PCCs exhibited stronger VEGFA-related angiogenic signaling, greater enrichment of stromal populations and MRC1+ M2-like macrophages, and more prominent LGALS9-CD45 signaling between macrophages and T cells. Our study provides single-cell insights into the tumor-intrinsic and microenvironmental heterogeneity between ACTH+CRH+ PCCs and ACTH-CRH- PCCs, revealing distinct tumor cell states and subtype-specific vascular and immune landscapes.

papers.title: Atypical presacral masses in Currarino syndrome: a case series.
papers.abstract: Currarino syndrome is a rare congenital disorder classically defined by the triad of sacral anomaly, anorectal malformation, and a presacral mass. While anterior meningoceles and teratomas are the most commonly reported lesions, an expanding body of literature suggests a broader spectrum of presacral pathology. We present three cases from our institution that expand the phenotypic range of presacral masses associated with Currarino syndrome, including lesions not previously well described in this population. Three cases are presented. Final pathologic diagnoses included myxopapillary ependymoma, mature cystic teratoma, and neuroendocrine tumor arising within a teratoma. These cases highlight the considerable heterogeneity of presacral lesions in Currarino syndrome and identify two underrecognized or previously unreported tumor types: myxopapillary ependymoma and neuroendocrine tumor. Surgical management must be individualized and often requires a multidisciplinary approach. Future studies will further clarify genotype-phenotype relationships and improve diagnostic and management strategies in this complex syndrome. Currarino syndrome is a rare congenital disorder classically defined by the triad of sacral anomaly, anorectal malformation, and a presacral mass. Presacral masses are most commonly anterior meningoceles and teratomas. A wider spectrum of lesions has been reported, underscoring the complexity of the syndrome and the importance of thorough evaluation and management of presacral pathology. In Case 1, we report a previously undescribed association of myxopapillary ependymoma with a retrorectal teratoma in the setting of Currarino syndrome. Case 2 illustrates the potential for significant enlargement of presacral meningoceles with associated teratomas with a rare instance of prenatal diagnosis by ultrasound. Case 3 expands the spectrum of presacral pathology in Currarino syndrome by demonstrating a neuroendocrine tumor.

papers.title: Circulating Extracellular Matrix Biomarkers in the Detection of Carcinoid Heart Disease.
papers.abstract: Carcinoid heart disease (CHD) is a severe fibrotic complication affecting cardiac valves in patients with neuroendocrine neoplasms (NEN). Early detection is crucial to improve prognosis. The value of the recommended screening biomarker, NT-proBNP, is uncertain. Biomarkers reflecting extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling may capture early fibrogenesis. We aimed to evaluate circulating ECM biomarkers for detection of CHD and to compare their performance with NT-proBNP. In this cross-sectional study, we prospectively included patients with disseminated small intestinal NEN (siNEN). We performed transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) for CHD diagnosis, and blood samples were analyzed for 10 ECM biomarkers. Biomarker levels were compared between patients with and without CHD, and diagnostic performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristics (AUROC). Among 98 patients, 16 (16%) had CHD. PRO-C3 levels were significantly elevated in patients with CHD compared with patients without CHD (median 19.3 ng/ml (IQR: 15.6-24.0) vs 14.3 ng/ml (IQR: 12.4-17.5), p = 0.002). The AUROC of PRO-C3 for CHD detection was 0.77 (95% CI: 0.64-0.90). At a cut-off level of 15.4 ng/ml, the sensitivity was 85 %, the specificity 56 %, the positive predictive value 27 %, and the negative predictive value 95 %. In the direct comparison between PRO-C3 and NT-proBNP, PRO-C3 did not outperform NT-proBNP (p = 0.09). PRO-C3, reflecting collagen type III formation, demonstrated good performance in CHD detection and may represent a complementary or potentially earlier marker than NT-proBNP. However, the performance of PRO-C3 was insufficient as a stand-alone tool, and further evaluation and exploration of new biomarkers in larger cohorts is required.

papers.title: Pituitary adenomas (PitNETs): molecular pathophysiology, targeted drug delivery strategies and clinical therapeutic outcomes.
papers.abstract: Pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (PitNETs), historically referred to as pituitary adenomas, comprise a heterogeneous group of neuroendocrine tumors with diverse hormonal phenotypes, molecular characteristics, and clinical behavior. Their management includes surgery, pharmacological therapy, radiotherapy, and, in selected refractory cases, systemic or molecularly targeted approaches. Advances in molecular endocrinology have identified recurrent alterations and dysregulated signaling networks, including GNAS, USP8, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and MAPK-associated pathways, that contribute to the biological heterogeneity of PitNETs. This review summarizes the molecular mechanisms underlying PitNET development and examines established pharmacological therapies, including dopamine agonists, somatostatin receptor ligands, growth hormone receptor antagonists, and temozolomide, with emphasis on their mechanisms and clinical evidence. Emerging molecularly targeted approaches, including mTOR inhibition, EGFR-associated targeting, anti-angiogenic therapy, and immune checkpoint inhibition, are discussed according to their current level of experimental and clinical evidence. The review also evaluates advanced drug-delivery strategies relevant to pituitary disease, including intranasal delivery, nanoparticle-based systems, liposomal carriers, receptor-targeted platforms, and sustained-release formulations. Particular attention is given to the distinction between clinically established delivery technologies and approaches that remain experimental or are supported primarily by evidence extrapolated from other therapeutic areas. Clinical trial evidence is further summarized to contextualize the efficacy, limitations, and translational status of current and emerging therapies. Together, these perspectives highlight the opportunities and remaining challenges in developing more precise pharmacological and drug-delivery strategies for the management of PitNETs.

papers.title: Increasing Detection of Early-Onset Rectal Neuroendocrine Neoplasms in the Era of Earlier Colorectal Cancer Screening.
papers.abstract: BackgroundThis study aimed to evaluate contemporary national trends in the presentation, management, and outcomes of early-onset rectal neuroendocrine neoplasms (EORNETs).MethodsA retrospective cohort analysis of patients <50 years who underwent surgery for rectal neuroendocrine neoplasms was performed using the National Cancer Database (NCDB) (2004-2023). Patients undergoing surgery were categorized as local tumor excision or radical resection. Five-year overall survival (OS) was estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis, and multivariable Cox proportional hazards analysis was used to identify factors associated with OS. A sensitivity analysis was also performed in the well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor subgroup.Results7285 patients were included; 6638 (91.1%) underwent local excision and 647 (8.9%) radical resection. The annual number of surgically treated cases increased from 234 in 2004 to 778 in 2023. 83.0% of tumors with known grade were low grade, and 90.6% of tumors with known clinical stage were stage I. Radical resection was associated with larger tumors, higher grade, more advanced stage, lymphovascular invasion, and liver metastases (all P < .001). Five-year OS was higher after local excision than radical resection (97.5% vs 85.7%, P < .001). In the full multivariable model, radical resection was associated with worse OS (HR 3.43, 95% CI 1.60-7.36; P = .002); however, this association was no longer statistically significant in the well-differentiated tumor subgroup (HR 2.52, 95% CI 0.97-6.54; P = .057).ConclusionsThe number of surgically treated EORNET cases substantially increased over time. Local excision was the predominant treatment. These findings are compatible with increased detection of indolent lesions through greater endoscopic evaluation.

papers.title: Approach to a patient with MEN1 syndrome.
papers.abstract: MEN1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1) is an uncommon, autosomal dominant inherited endocrine tumour predisposition syndrome. The most common manifestations of MEN1 are primary hyperparathyroidism, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours and pituitary adenomas. Individuals with MEN1 benefit from lifelong surveillance, with the aim of detecting MEN1 manifestations early. The ideal timepoint for interventions needs to be carefully selected in the context of the syndrome. Published guidelines help clinicians to navigate the management and follow up of individuals with MEN1. This article aims to explore some of the nuance in the investigation and management of this often complex condition from an endocrinologist's point of view, through exploration of 4 clinical case vignettes.
papers.journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

papers.title: [Calcitonin measurement in fine needle aspiration washout fluid : when biology arbitrates between two cytological diagnoses].
papers.abstract: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is a lesion whose preoperative diagnosis mainly relies on serum calcitonin measurement and cytology obtained by fine-needle aspiration. A marked elevation of calcitonin during the evaluation of a thyroid nodule constitutes a warning signal. The sensitivity of cytology is limited because of the tumor's morphological heterogeneity. Measurement of calcitonin in the washout fluid from the aspiration needle and syringe significantly improves diagnostic performance, both for thyroid nodules and for suspicious lymph nodes. This clinical vignette illustrates the importance of integrating biological and cytological data to optimize the initial management. It raises several questions: What is the role of serum calcitonin measurement in the evaluation of thyroid nodules? Why can cytology miss the diagnosis of medullary carcinoma? What benefits does measuring calcitonin in fine-needle aspiration washout fluid provide? Finally, how can the accuracy of the preoperative diagnosis influence the surgical strategy ?

papers.title: Adrenal Masses in a Moroccan Tertiary Center: A 14-Year Retrospective Study of 200 Patients.
papers.abstract: Objectives Adrenal masses are increasingly detected and encompass a broad spectrum of clinical presentations and pathological diagnoses. This study aimed to describe the epidemiological, clinical, paraclinical, etiological, and therapeutic profiles of patients with adrenal masses. Materials and methods This single-center retrospective descriptive study included consecutive eligible patients hospitalized for adrenal masses at the Department of Endocrinology, Diabetology, Metabolic Diseases, and Nutrition of Hassan II University Hospital in Fez, Morocco, between January 2009 and January 2023. Data were retrospectively collected from medical records between January and February 2023. Results A total of 200 patients were included, with a mean age of 49 years and a predominance of female patients (n = 142, 71%). The most common circumstance of discovery was adrenal incidentaloma (n = 110, 55%). The etiological diagnoses were non-secreting adenoma (n = 73, 36.5%), pheochromocytoma (n = 33, 16.5%), Conn's adenoma (n = 22, 11%), cortisol-secreting adenoma (n = 20, 10%), adrenocortical carcinoma (n = 18, 9%), adrenal metastases (n = 13, 6.5%), adrenal cysts (n = 7, 3.5%), lymphoma (n = 5, 2.5%), myelolipoma (n = 4, 2%), ganglioneuroma (n = 2, 1%), schwannoma (n = 2, 1%), and oncocytic adenoma (n = 1, 0.5%). Surgical treatment was performed in 80 patients (40%), documented clinical and biological surveillance was performed in 43 patients (21.5%), and 10 patients (5%) received palliative treatment. Conclusion This study demonstrates the diversity of adrenal mass etiologies and clinical presentations and highlights the importance of a multidisciplinary diagnostic and therapeutic approach.

papers.title: Survival after lymph node dissection, radiotherapy, and combined treatment in sentinel node-positive stage IIIA Merkel cell carcinoma: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) has a high risk of regional lymphatic metastasis. In cases of lymphatic micrometastasis, an evidence-based clinical approach is missing. To assess survival outcomes following complete lymph node dissection (CLND), radiation (RTX), or CLND plus RTX (CLND + RTX) in patients with stage IIIA MCC. A systematic search was conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library. Pooled survival rates were calculated using random-effects models. Comparative effectiveness of interventions was assessed via network meta-analysis. Eight studies, including 1825 patients, were analyzed. Pooled 1- and 3-year survival rates (overall survival and MCC-specific survival) following CLND (regardless of RTX) were 93% (95% CI, 89%-96%) and 71% (95% CI, 64%-77%), showing no significant difference compared with patients without CLND. Furthermore, relative risk ratios comparing RTX (regardless of CLND status) with no RTX demonstrated no significant differences for overall survival at either 1 or 3 years. Finally, a network meta-analysis also did not show superiority among CLND only, RTX only, and CLND + RTX in patients with stage IIIA MCC. The limited number of observational studies, data heterogeneity, missing data regarding immunotherapies, and low evidence levels according to the GRADE restrict definitive conclusions. Findings underscore the need for large, prospective clinical trials to define optimal treatment strategies for patients with stage IIIA MCC. CRD42025636348.

papers.title: Spatial Atlas of Small Cell Lung Carcinoma Reveals Intratumoral Tumor-State Heterogeneity and an MMP12+ Macrophage Niche.
papers.abstract: Small-cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) is a highly aggressive tumor with a dismal prognosis among lung cancers. Treatment is failing because of primary or rapidly developing secondary resistance. Recent molecular studies have suggested four SCLC subtypes with unique therapeutic vulnerabilities-ASCL1, NEUROD1, POU2F3, and YAP. These subtypes still distinguish themselves by considerable intra-tumoral heterogeneity and the influence of the microenvironmental context, which are both considered to be responsible for treatment resistance. We integrated in situ hybridization-based spatial transcriptomics with histological and protein-expression analyses of 18 specimens, comprising 16 SCLCs, one atypical carcinoid, and one normal lung specimen. Systematic case-by-case analysis revealed multiple coexisting tumor states, including neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine components, regional hypoxic states, and case-specific FABP7-positive and loss-of-chromosome-Y-associated populations. Integrative transcriptome clustering, copy number estimation, and exploratory trajectory analysis revealed transcriptional relationships among spatially coexisting tumor states, including phenotypically distinct tumor components with molecular features consistent with close clonal relationships in selected heterogeneous tumors. Furthermore, we identified immune signatures and uncovered a previously unrecognized MMP12-positive tumor-associated macrophage population, enriched at the tumor interface and spatially associated with necrotic and hypoxic regions. In vitro co-culture experiments further showed that direct contact with SCLC cells increased MMP12 expression in macrophages, with hypoxia further enhancing its expression under specific conditions. Together, our study delineates the complex spatial architecture of SCLC by defining specific cellular programs and adjacent immune phenotypes that provide an organizational framework for understanding its marked intratumoral heterogeneity.

papers.title: Immune-Excluded Mucosal Melanoma: Spatial Mechanisms of Checkpoint Resistance and Biomarker-Guided Therapeutic Opportunities.
papers.abstract: Mucosal melanoma is a rare, aggressive melanoma subtype arising from melanocytes within mucosal surfaces of the head and neck, anorectal, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts. Unlike ultraviolet-driven cutaneous melanoma, mucosal melanoma has lower tumor mutational burden, fewer BRAF V600 alterations, greater structural genomic complexity, and recurrent drivers including mutations in KIT, NRAS, NF1, SF3B1, and copy-number alterations. It is often diagnosed at advanced stages, recurs locally, disseminates early, and responds less favorably to immune checkpoint inhibition than cutaneous melanoma. Low neoantigen burden contributes to this resistance, but emerging evidence indicates that antitumor immunity is also shaped by spatially organized tumor-immune interactions, site-specific mucosal biology, suppressive myeloid and stromal programs, angiogenic signaling, and underexplored innate checkpoint pathways. Here, we review mucosal melanoma as a biologically distinct model of immune-excluded melanoma, summarizing its clinical behavior, genomic architecture, immunotherapy outcomes, and mechanisms of checkpoint resistance, with emphasis on restricted intratumoral CD8-positive T-cell infiltration, macrophage- and stroma-rich barriers, angiogenic remodeling, and candidate innate checkpoints including B7-H3, CD24-Siglec-10, CD47-SIRPα, and B7-H6/NKp30. We further discuss how spatial and circulating biomarkers may support response-adapted translational studies and define actionable immune states across mucosal melanoma sites.

papers.title: PD-1 inhibitor-associated Sicca syndrome mimicking Sjögren's disease successfully managed without immunotherapy withdrawal.
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are increasingly associated with a broad spectrum of immune-related adverse events (irAEs), including rheumatic manifestations. We report a case of ICI-associated sicca syndrome (ICI-S) mimicking Sjögren's disease, with a brief literature review. The patient was a 70-year-old man with BRAF-mutated metastatic melanoma who developed inflammatory arthralgias followed by parotid and submandibular enlargement, severe xerostomia, and xerophthalmia, during pembrolizumab therapy. Treatment was withheld and low-dose glucocorticoids (GC) initiated, with rapid improvement of joint symptoms and gland swelling, although marked xerostomia persisted. The diagnostic work-up revealed elevated inflammatory markers and positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA), with negative anti-SSA/SSB. Salivary gland ultrasound showed grade 3 changes (OMERACT) and PET-CT confirmed bilateral sialadenitis. Minor salivary gland biopsy demonstrated T-cell-predominant lymphocytic infiltrate without CD20+ B cells, supporting an ICI-S rather than primary Sjögren's disease. Pembrolizumab rechallenge triggered a flare of sialadenitis and arthritis, controlled with GC reintroduction plus hydroxychloroquine and supportive measures. This case provides educational insights into the diagnostic differentiation between ICI-S and primary Sjögren's disease, supporting early recognition and appropriate management without compromising oncologic treatment.

papers.title: Synergistic antitumor effects of 5-fluorouracil and vorinostat in preclinical models of pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas.
papers.abstract: Therapeutic options for metastatic pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas (PPGLs) are largely limited, highlighting the need for novel strategies. This study aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) and vorinostat (SAHA), alone or in combination in preclinical PPGL models. The growth inhibitory effects of 5-FU and SAHA were investigated in PC-12 cells and human PPGL primary cultures (n = 4) using CCK-8 assays. Drug interactions were evaluated utilizing the Chou-Talalay method. Specific mechanisms were explored via flow cytometry, wound healing, and transwell assays. In vivo efficacy and safety were assessed using mouse subcutaneous xenograft models. Both monotherapies inhibited PC-12 growth in a dose- and time-dependent manner (5-FU: 0-160 μM and SAHA: 0-80 μM). The combination therapy (20 μM 5-FU + 10 μM SAHA) exhibited a robust synergistic effect with the combination index < 1, achieving 43% growth inhibition in PC-12 cells and nearly 70% in primary cultures, significantly outperforming monotherapies. This combination significantly exacerbated G0/G1 cell cycle arrest and suppressed PC-12 cell migration and invasion. In vivo, the combined treatment reduced final tumor volumes by approximately 50% and significantly decreased the Ki-67 index. Despite mild body weight loss on days 15 and 21, no evident histopathological organ damage was observed. This study provides the first preclinical evidence that combining SAHA with 5-FU exerts a robust synergistic antitumor effect in PPGLs with no evident histopathological organ damage, laying a strong foundation for developing novel combination therapy for metastatic PPGLs.

papers.title: Association of obstructive sleep apnea with pancreatic cancer in high-risk patients under surveillance in CAPS and PCYST cohorts.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) has been linked with increased cancer incidence and mortality. We hypothesized that OSA may be a risk factor for neoplastic progression among patients undergoing pancreatic cancer surveillance. Retrospective medical record review of two Johns Hopkins Hospital cohorts undergoing pancreas surveillance; patients with familial/genetic risk enrolled in the Cancer of the Pancreas Screening (CAPS) study and patients with incidentally detected pancreatic cysts, enrolled in the PCYST study. Time-to-progression to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and neoplastic progression (either PDAC, high-grade dysplasia or pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor) were compared by OSA status, adjusting for covariates. OSA was diagnosed prior to or during surveillance in 174 (19.5%) of 893 patients in CAPS and 376 (23.7%) of 1585 patients in the PCYST cohort. In the combined cohorts, OSA was associated with increased risk of progression to PDAC (unadjusted HR: 3.12, 95% CI: [1.82, 5.34], p < 0.001). OSA was also associated with male sex, higher BMI, fatty liver, fatty pancreas, diabetes, and history of smoking (all p < 0.01). After covariate adjustment, OSA remained associated with PDAC risk (adjusted HR: 2.56 [1.44, 4.55], p = 0.001). Factors associated with neoplastic progression included OSA (adjusted HR: 1.93 [1.25, 2.97], p = 0.003), increasing age (age-per 5-years adjusted HR: 1.14 [1.05, 1.24], p = 0.003), fatty liver (adjusted HR: 1.76 [1.19, 2.60], p = 0.005), and diabetes (adjusted HR: 1.77 [1.16, 2.71], p = 0.008). Patients undergoing pancreatic surveillance for their familial/genetic risk and/or incidentally detected pancreatic cysts have a greater likelihood of developing pancreatic cancer if they've been diagnosed with OSA.

papers.title: Crossing the Threshold to Emergency Surgery: Robot-Assisted Adrenalectomy for Refractory Pheochromocytoma Crisis.
papers.abstract: Pheochromocytoma crisis can make conventional adrenergic preparation impossible and force consideration of adrenalectomy before physiologic recovery. This narrative review synthesizes the evidence that informs the transition from continued stabilization to nondeferrable tumor removal. Emergency presentation alone does not constitute an operative indication. When hemorrhage is controlled and cardiovascular and extracardiac organ function improved, surgery should be deferred until preparation is completed. Uncontrolled bleeding, expanding hematoma, or life-threatening compression requires immediate source-control assessment. Transcatheter arterial embolization may provide a bridge to elective adrenalectomy in selected hemorrhagic presentations. In nonhemorrhagic crisis, rescue adrenalectomy may be considered only when serial multidisciplinary reassessment shows persistent tumor-driven deterioration despite appropriate support, conventional preparation cannot be advanced safely, the lesion is localized and resectable, and organ injury remains potentially reversible. Mechanical circulatory support usually serves as a bridge to myocardial recovery and later surgery rather than as a routine platform for adrenalectomy. No validated temporal, hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-failure threshold defines the point at which surgery becomes preferable to continued support. Operative access should therefore be selected only after the indication for surgery has been established and should reflect anatomy, physiologic tolerance, institutional expertise, and immediate conversion capability.

papers.title: Testosterone and DHEA-S Secreting Adrenal Cortical Adenoma in a Postmenopausal Woman: A Rare Functional Incidentaloma.
papers.abstract: Postmenopausal hyperandrogenism is uncommon and should prompt evaluation for an underlying androgen-secreting source. Although ovarian causes are more frequent, adrenal tumors remain an important consideration and may occasionally be malignant. We report a 53-year-old postmenopausal woman who presented with progressive hirsutism, scalp hair loss, and mild clitoromegaly. Laboratory evaluation showed markedly elevated total testosterone and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate levels with suppressed gonadotropins. Pelvic ultrasonography showed no ovarian mass. CT demonstrated a 3.5 × 2.4 cm left adrenal mass with precontrast attenuation of 31 Hounsfield units and an enhancement washout pattern not typical of an adrenal adenoma. MRI showed a 3.6 × 2.1 cm left adrenal lesion with arterial hyperenhancement, restricted diffusion, and no signal drop on out-of-phase imaging. Biochemical testing excluded pheochromocytoma, primary aldosteronism, and clinically significant cortisol co-secretion. The patient underwent laparoscopic adrenalectomy, and pathology confirmed a 3.6 cm adrenal cortical adenoma with negative margins, positive inhibin, Melan-A, and steroidogenic factor-1 staining, and Ki-67 <3%. Postoperative androgen levels normalized, and adrenal insufficiency was excluded by cosyntropin stimulation testing. This case highlights the importance of integrating clinical presentation, biochemical localization, adrenal imaging, differential diagnosis, and pathology when evaluating severe postmenopausal hyperandrogenism.

papers.title: Coexisting focal nodular hyperplasia and diffuse hepatic metastases from an ileal neuroendocrine tumor: a case report and literature review.
papers.abstract: Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) is a benign liver lesion usually associated with vascular abnormalities. Neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), on the other hand, frequently metastasize to the liver and typically appear as hypervascular lesions. The coexistence of FNH and diffuse hepatic metastases from an ileal NET is exceptionally rare and represents a major diagnostic challenge because both entities may present as hypervascular liver lesions, potentially leading to misdiagnosis and inappropriate management. A 56-year-old woman with a history of epilepsy treated with sodium valproate presented with progressive right upper quadrant pain and abdominal distension. Imaging showed a large hepatic lesion suggestive of FNH along with multiple hypervascular liver nodules suspicious for metastases. A CT-guided liver biopsy demonstrated metastatic well-differentiated NET with a Ki-67 index below 2%. Laboratory tests revealed elevated chromogranin A and urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid levels. The patient also had chronic diarrhea and moderate tricuspid regurgitation consistent with carcinoid syndrome. A ^68 Ga-DOTANOC positron emission tomography/computed tomography localized the primary tumor to the ileum. The integration of radiological, functional, and histopathological findings enabled accurate diagnosis and appropriate therapeutic planning. Surgical resection of the primary tumor was performed, followed by long-acting octreotide therapy. The patient remained clinically stable, with no progression of the hepatic lesions during follow-up. The presence of multiple hypervascular liver lesions in patients with NETs raises important diagnostic issues, especially when benign and malignant lesions coexist. This case demonstrates the value of integrating hepatobiliary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), histopathological confirmation, and functional imaging to accurately distinguish FNH from metastatic disease and to guide appropriate therapeutic management. The coexistence of FNH and diffuse liver metastases from an ileal NET is rare. This case highlights the pivotal role of a multimodal diagnostic approach combining hepatobiliary MRI, functional imaging, and targeted histopathological confirmation to distinguish benign from malignant hypervascular liver lesions, avoid diagnostic pitfalls, and optimize patient management.

papers.title: Mixed adenoneuroendocrine carcinoma (MANEC) of the ampulla of Vater with sarcomatosis: a case report.
papers.abstract: Biliary mixed neuroendocrine-non-neuroendocrine neoplasms (MiNENs) are rare, accounting for only 4-24% of all intestinal MiNENs. Diagnosing them preoperatively remains challenging due to the limitations of biopsy and imaging. As a result, the optimal treatment strategy, particularly for postoperative management, is still poorly defined. A 61-year-old woman presented to the Surgical Department of Sfax General Hospital on 23 December 2021, with a 1-month history of jaundice, yellow discoloration of the eyes and urine, and clay-colored stools. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed dilated intra- and extrahepatic biliary ducts without evidence of stones or masses in the common bile duct. A positron emission tomography scan confirmed peritoneal and thoracic adenomegaly. The patient underwent a cephalic pancreatoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure). Histopathological examination of the surgical specimen confirmed a MiNEN. This case is particularly noteworthy for its rare association of a biliary MiNEN with a sarcomatoid component. This case highlights the diagnostic and therapeutic complexities of biliary MiNENs. Given their rarity, sharing evidence-based clinical experiences is vital to standardize practices and improve patient outcomes. This report emphasizes the need for a multidisciplinary approach and thorough histopathological analysis to ensure accurate diagnosis and tailored management.

papers.title: Unicentric hyaline-vascular Castleman disease of the jejunal mesentery mimicking a gastrointestinal stromal tumor or neuroendocrine tumor: a case report.
papers.abstract: Castleman disease (CD) is a rare lymphoproliferative disorder classified as unicentric (UCD) or multicentric (MCD). The hyaline vascular variant of UCD most commonly arises in the mediastinum, whereas mesenteric involvement is exceedingly rare. As it can mimic hypervascular mesenteric tumors like neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) and gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs), preoperative diagnosis remains challenging. A 36-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of vague abdominal discomfort, early satiety, and an unintentional 9-kg weight loss. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a hypervascular jejunal mesenteric mass of size 2.0 × 1.7 cm, suspicious for a NET or GIST. Owing to the diagnostic uncertainty, exploratory laparoscopy converted to a mini-laparotomy with en bloc resection of the mesenteric mass and an adjacent 10-cm segment of jejunum was performed. Histopathological and immunohistochemical examination confirmed hyaline vascular unicentric CD. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient remained asymptomatic with complete weight recovery and no evidence of recurrence at 12-month follow-up. Mesenteric unicentric CD is a rare but important differential diagnosis of solitary hypervascular intra-abdominal masses. As imaging findings often mimic mesenchymal and NETs, definitive diagnosis relies on histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluation. Complete surgical resection is both diagnostic and curative for localized disease.

papers.title: Non-ampullary duodenal mixed neuroendocrine-non-neuroendocrine neoplasm initially diagnosed as adenocarcinoma: a case report.
papers.abstract: Mixed neuroendocrine-non-neuroendocrine neoplasms (MiNENs) are rare tumors composed of neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine components. Their occurrence in the duodenum is extremely uncommon. Preoperative diagnosis is difficult because the neuroendocrine component may not be detected in biopsy specimens. We report a rare case of non-ampullary duodenal MiNEN initially diagnosed as adenocarcinoma. A 56-year-old man was found to have a tumor in the duodenal bulb during routine endoscopic examination. Biopsy revealed moderately to poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma, and computed tomography demonstrated bulky regional lymph node metastasis without distant disease. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with S-1 plus oxaliplatin was administered based on treatment strategies used for advanced gastric cancer in Japan. Post-treatment evaluation showed stable disease, and pancreaticoduodenectomy with regional lymph node dissection achieved R0 resection. Histopathological examination revealed both adenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC) components, leading to a diagnosis of MiNEN. Lymph node metastases demonstrated component-specific heterogeneity, with NEC involvement in station No. 8a and adenocarcinoma in the remaining metastatic nodes. Postoperative platinum-based chemotherapy was administered, and the patient remains recurrence-free at 16 months after surgery. Duodenal MiNEN presents diagnostic and therapeutic challenges because biopsy specimens may fail to detect the neuroendocrine component preoperatively. In the present case, component-specific lymph node metastases suggested biological heterogeneity and may have influenced treatment selection. Non-ampullary duodenal MiNEN is a rare and diagnostically challenging disease. This case highlights the importance of accurate pathological evaluation and multidisciplinary management.

papers.title: Primary large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the submandibular gland arising from a long-standing benign tumor: case report.
papers.abstract: Large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) is an aggressive malignancy that commonly arises in the lungs. Primary salivary gland involvement is exceptional, presenting a major diagnostic challenge in differentiating it from metastatic pulmonary disease. A 62-year-old man presented with a right submandibular mass that had been stable for 16 years before rapidly expanding. Imaging revealed a massive 11 cm necrotic submandibular tumor with disseminated pulmonary and hepatic metastases. Following partial debulking, pathology revealed a high-grade neuroendocrine tumor (Ki-67 index 85%) arising alongside a benign mesenchymal component. Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse CD56 positivity and TTF-1 negativity. While histology mimics pulmonary variants, the dominant pre-existing cervical mass and chronologic evolution strongly suggest a primary salivary origin, likely representing malignant transformation of a benign lesion. This case highlights the rare phenomenon of primary salivary LCNEC developing within a long-standing benign mass. It underscores the importance of including high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma in the differential diagnosis of rapidly expanding salivary lesions.

Mesenteric Adhesion and Poorer Perioperative Outcomes in Gastric Submucosal Tumors: A Retrospective Study of Endoscopic Full-Thickness Resection
papers.abstract: Background Endoscopic full-thickness resection(EFTR) has become an increasingly common method for treating gastric submucosal tumors (SMTs). Adhesion between the SMT and the adjacent mesentery represents an intraoperative challenge that can affect the perioperative clinical outcomes for patients. Objective The aim of this study was to analyze the risk factors for SMT–mesentery adhesion and the effect of SMT–mesentery adhesion on perioperative clinical outcomes. Methods We retrospectively reviewed the information of patients with gastric SMTs who underwent EFTR in our center from January 2022 to August 2026. Patients were divided into adhesion and non-adhesion groups. Perioperative clinical outcomes were compared between the two groups, and risk factors for SMT–mesentery adhesion were analyzed. Results A total of 202 patients were enrolled, and mesenteric adhesion was observed in 64 patients (31.7%). The adhesion group had significantly longer operative time (P < 0.001), greater elevation in white blood cell count (P < 0.001), and higher total hospitalization costs (P < 0.001). Multivariable logistic regression analysis revealed that tumors located on the posterior gastric wall (OR = 4.110, 95% CI: 1.855–9.105, P < 0.001), maximum diameter > 30 mm (OR = 7.449, 95% CI: 2.499–22.403, P < 0.001), and extraluminal growth pattern (OR = 15.571, 95% CI: 5.803–41.781, P < 0.001) were independent risk factors for tumor–mesentery adhesion, whereas hypertension (OR = 0.396, 95% CI: 0.178–0.880, P = 0.023) was a protective factor. Conclusion Mesenteric adhesion is a significant predictor of worse perioperative outcomes following EFTR for gastric SMTs, underscoring the importance of thorough preoperative assessment. Accordingly, EFTR should be approached with caution in patients with imaging evidence of mesenteric adhesion.

papers.title: Synchronous Medullary Carcinoma and Primary Follicular Lymphoma in the Same Thyroid Lobe: A Case Report and Literature Review
papers.abstract: Primary thyroid lymphoma (PTL) and medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) are rare malignancies. Their synchronous development as a collision tumor within a single thyroid lobe is exceptionally uncommon. We present a unique case of a 53-year-old female with a long-standing history of autoimmune thyroiditis who was simultaneously diagnosed with MTC and primary follicular lymphoma (FL, grade 3b) following histological examination of a surgical specimen. The diagnosis was confirmed using immunohistochemistry. Notably, the lymphoma cells lacked BCL2 expression despite a high histological grade, characteristic of a specific localized subgroup of extranodal FLs. This case highlights the critical importance of comprehensive histological and immunohistochemical evaluation of thyroid nodules, particularly in patients with chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, to guide optimal therapeutic management.

Diagnostic and Perioperative Complexity when Retroperitoneal Hemangioma Mimics Sympathetic Paraganglioma: A Case Report
papers.abstract: Background. Primary retroperitoneal tumors, which comprise 0.1–0.2% of all malignancies, can encompass various etiologies, and possess nonspecific imaging features. These factors make them a diagnosis of exclusion, especially in adult patients. Additionally, fewer than 50 cases of adult primary cavernous hemangiomas in the retroperitoneal space have been reported. However, when a hypervascular retroperitoneal mass is accompanied by hypertension and ambivalent serum catecholamine levels, a functional sympathetic paraganglioma becomes the leading diagnosis as it requires a differential work up, driving a high-stakes perioperative pathway. Case Presentation. A 52-year-old man with insulin dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and schizoaffective disorder had a well vascularized retroperitoneal mass incidentally identified on trauma imaging following a motor vehicular accident (MVA). Cross-sectional imaging and mildly-to-moderately elevated urinary and plasma catecholamines/Metanephrines raised concern for a functional paraganglioma. He underwent preoperative alpha then beta-adrenergic blockade and laparoscopic resection. Final Histopathology demonstrated a cavernous hemangioma with no neuroendocrine tissue. Conclusions. The combination of chronic hypertension, anxiety, and equivocal biochemistry produced a convincing phenotype for functional paraganglioma. Since unprepared resection of a functional paraganglioma carries substantial perioperative cardiovascular risk, alpha-blockade optimization was justified even though the lesion proved non-functional. Poorly controlled diabetes with marked perioperative glycemic variability added independent surgical risk. Since hypervascular retroperitoneal masses are rare in adults; if the diagnosis of a functional paraganglioma cannot be excluded, the safest course is to prepare as though the mass were one.

papers.title: Preemptive interdural dissection in endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery for cavernous sinus medial wall resection: A technical note with step-by-step illustration
papers.abstract: Objective Microscopic invasion of the cavernous sinus (CS) medial wall is a major cause of surgical failure and persistent hormone hypersecretion in functioning pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (PitNETs). This study provides a step-by-step description of an endoscopic transsphenoidal technique for selective CS medial wall resection, emphasizing preemptive development of the interdural plane before tumor removal to facilitate controlled entry into the CS and subsequent medial wall mobilization. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 10 patients with functioning PitNETs who underwent endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery with CS medial wall resection between January 2020 and June 2024 at three institutions. The procedure involved developing an interdural plane at the inferolateral sellar region before tumor removal, followed by stepwise mobilization and detachment of the medial wall. Clinical, radiologic, and endocrinologic outcomes were evaluated. Results Gross total resection was achieved in all patients. The mean intraoperative blood loss was 158 mL (range, 70–200 mL). Three patients experienced intraoperative cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage, which was successfully managed with multilayer closure. No postoperative CSF leaks, vascular injuries, or new permanent cranial neuropathies were observed. At a median follow-up of 21 (range, 14–36) months, biochemical remission was achieved in nine patients. Conclusions Preemptive interdural dissection during endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery provides an anatomically guided strategy for controlled entry into the CS and subsequent medial wall mobilization. This approach may facilitate CS medial wall resection while minimizing unnecessary manipulation near critical neurovascular structures in selected patients with functioning PitNETs.

papers.title: Carotid Body Paraganglioma Presenting With Paroxysmal Hypertension: A Case Report
papers.abstract:
Background: Carotid body paragangliomas（CBP）generally lack clinical manifestations of catecholamine excess. some patients may exhibit a dopaminergic biochemical phenotype characterized by elevated dopamine levels. Case Report: We report a patient with a CBP who presented with paroxysmal hypertension and recurrent syncope. Biochemical evaluation revealed elevated plasma dopamine and 3-methoxytyramine (3-MT) levels, whereas other catecholamines remained within the reference ranges. The symptoms improved following tumor resection.

Discussion:

Elevated dopamine alone cannot fully explain the paroxysmal hypertension. Transient catecholamine release during symptomatic episodes may have contributed. Because dynamic monitoring during episodes and postoperative biochemical reassessment were unavailable, the underlying mechanism remains unclear.

Conclusion:

Dopaminergic CBP may exhibit heterogeneous hemodynamic presentations. Individualized preoperative assessment based on the patient’s clinical presentation may help optimize perioperative management.

papers.title: Data-efficient machine learning for the detection of duodenal neoplasia: a multi-centre study
papers.abstract:
Background

Machine Learning (ML) has shown promise in histopathological diagnosis, but rare tumours, like duodenal epithelial neoplasms, are challenging because large, labelled datasets are difficult to assemble. We propose a data-efficient ML pipeline for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia in whole-slide images.

Methods

We assembled a five-hospital dataset of haematoxylin and eosin–stained duodenal biopsy whole slide images (WSIs) at 10x magnification, comprising 8,027 normal and 401 neoplastic biopsies, including adenomas, carcinomas and neuroendocrine tumours. WSIs were divided into patches and encoded using the Hibou-B foundation model. We compared global standardisation with unsupervised site-specific standardisation of patch embeddings. Our pipeline combined principal component analysis, a Gaussian mixture model and a Random Forest classifier. We assessed generalisability using leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation across four hospitals and on an independent test set from a fifth hospital.

Results

In leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation, the pipeline achieved a mean accuracy of 90%, sensitivity of 96%, specificity of 83% and an AUC of 0.96. On the external test hospital, it achieved 94% accuracy, 93% sensitivity, 95% specificity, and AUC of 0.97. Site-specific standardisation improved mean cross-validation accuracy by 20 percentage points compared with global standardisation, while the Gaussian mixture pipeline improved accuracy by 12 percentage points compared with mean pooling of patch embeddings.

Conclusions

We present a data-efficient ML approach for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia from WSIs. Strong performance was maintained across hospitals and on an independent external test cohort despite the limited number of neoplastic training cases, supporting the feasibility of foundation-model-based approaches for rare histopathological diagnoses.

papers.title: Safety and Efficacy of Dosimetry-Guided 177Lu-DOTATATE Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy in Advanced GEP-NETs: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: Purpose Currently, standard peptide receptor radiation therapy (PRRT) with 177Lu-DOTATATE is used with a fixed-dose regimen (4 × 7.4 GBq) that aims to help limit radiation exposure to vital organs but often undertreats patients. [1] In addition, the use of personalized therapeutic doses is thought to be highly toxic. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the safety and efficacy of PRRT with personalized, dose-guided doses in patients with advanced gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NETs). Methods An extensive and systematic literature search was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines to identify fit-for-purpose trials, using personalized doses based on the PRRT organ. The primary outcomes were severe nephrotoxicity and hematology (grades 3–4), objective response rate (ORR), and progression-free survival (PFS). The methodological and research reliability of the selected trial was evaluated using the RoB 2 and MINORS tools. The aggregate rate was calculated using a random effect model with the Freeman-Tukey dual arc transformation. Results Two prospective clinical trials (randomized phase 2, single-handed phase II) included 152 patients who met the inclusion criteria. Both studies increased the cumulative biologic dose (BED) to the kidneys up to 27–40 Gy, which still showed safety. The overall rate of grade 3–4 nephrotoxicity was 0.0% (95% confidence interval: 0.00–0.00; I² = 0%). The overall rate of grade 3–4 hematological toxicity was 9.2% (95% confidence interval: 0.05–0.15; I² = 0%). Long-term efficacy from the phase II group showed an ORR of 16%, a disease control rate of 78%, a median PFS of 29 months, and an overall survival of 47 to 53 months. Conclusion Dosimetry-guided 177Lu-DOTATATE therapy with individualized doses has been shown to be safe and feasible. By safely and controllably exceeding conventional nephrotoxic threshold limits, personalized PRRT helps optimize radiation therapy for tumors, prevent insufficient dose treatment, and provide long-term, sustainable life benefits without increasing severe toxicity.

papers.abstract: High-grade gliomas (HGGs), including astrocytoma and glioblastoma (GBM), constitute the most prevalent primary tumors of the central nervous system (CNS). GBM cells demonstrate a notable ability to infiltrate the brain parenchyma, precluding complete surgical resection. Here we investigated the spreading of GBM cells and the response of the CNS microenvironment focusing on glial cells, which are essential interactors to GBM. We used acute and organotypic slices from the mouse brain and peritumoral cortex of patients with HGGs. We found that human peritumoral tissue from cortical resection was characterized by high levels of the astrocytic Connexin43 protein (Cx43) and discrete infiltration of microglia. In contrast, the tumor core exhibited high myeloid infiltration and an altered extracellular matrix (ECM) composition, which was poor in CD44. We tracked mouse and primary human-labeled-GBM cells in 2D cultures and in co-culture with organotypic slices generated from mouse brain and human peritumoral tissues. We found that the implanted GBM cells infiltrated the brain tissue, implying early glial modifications including an increase in Cx43 expression and distribution. Furthermore, the blockage of Cx43 hemichannels was accompanied by morphological changes and polarization of human GBM cells, typical for migration phenomena. The present study sheds light on the dynamics of GBM cells spreading in the living brain tissue, suggesting that the progression of the tumor correlates with changes within the host brain. Our findings identify the upregulation of Cx43 expression as a highly consistent modification in both mouse and human tissue that may be crucial for GBM infiltration.

trials.brief:
Background:

Neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs) are rare cancers in the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, lungs, adrenal glands, and other areas of the body. Many of these cancers have a high risk of relapse and a low chance of survival. Better treatments are needed.

Objective:

To test a new drug, ADCT-701, in people with NENs.

Eligibility:

Adults aged 18 and older with NENs.

Design:

Participants will be screened. They will have a physical exam with blood and urine tests. They will have imaging scans and tests of heart functioning. Their ability to perform normal daily activities will be tested. A biopsy may be needed: A sample of tissue will be removed from the tumor.

ADCT-701 is given through a tube attached to a needle inserted into a vein in the arm. Participants will receive the drug treatment on the first day of 21-day treatment cycles. They will visit the clinic a total of 10 times during the first two cycles. After that, they will visit the clinic 2 times during each cycle. Gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumors (GI NET) are a type of cancer that affects the stomach and intestines; pheochromocytoma/paragangliomas (PPGL) are tumors that grow in or near the adrenal glands. Both of these types of tumor have high levels of a protein called somatostatin receptors (SSTR) on their surfaces. Researchers want to test a treatment that targets SSTR.

To test a drug (\[212Pb\]VMT-alpha-NET) in people with GI NET or PPGL. The drug has 2 components: a protein to bind to SSTR and a radioactive agent to kill the cancer cells.

Adults aged 18 years or older with GI NET or PPGL tumors that have spread and cannot be removed with surgery.

They will remain in the clinic at least 4 hours after each infusion and may need to stay in the hospital for up to 48 hour for monitoring and testing. Some participants will also get a related study drug (\[203Pb\]VMT-alpha-NET). They will receive this drug a few days before the first 2 cycles. At 4, 24, and 48 hours after each infusion, they will have whole body scans. These scans will show where the study drug went in their body.

trials.brief:
Background:

A person s tumor is studied for mutations. When cells are found that can attack the mutation in a person s tumor, the genes from those cells are studied to find the parts that make the attack possible. White blood cells are then taken from the person s body, and the gene transfer occurs in a laboratory. A type of virus is used to transfer the genes that make those white blood cells able to attack the mutation in the tumor. The gene transfer therapy is the return of those white blood cells back to the person.

Objective:

To see if gene transfer therapy of white blood cells can shrink tumors.

Eligibility:

People with certain metastatic cancer for which standard treatments have not worked.

Design:

Participants may complete screening under another protocol. Screening includes:

* Getting tumor cells from a previous procedure
* Medical history
* Physical exam
* Scans
* Blood, urine, heart, and lung tests

The study has 8 stages:

1. Screening tests repeated over 1-2 weeks. Participants will have leukapheresis: Blood is removed by a needle in one arm. A machine removes white blood cells. The rest of the blood is returned by a needle in the other arm.
2. Care at home over approximately 12 weeks.
3. Stopping therapy for 4-6 weeks while their cells are changed in a lab.
4. Hospital stay approximately 3-4 weeks for treatment. An IV catheter will be placed in the chest to administer drugs.
5. Patients on Arm 2 of the study will receive the first dose of pembrolizumab while in the hospital. Three additional doses will be given after the cell infusion 3 weeks apart.
6. Receiving changed cells by catheter. Then getting a drug over 1-5 days to help the cells live longer.
7. Recover in the hospital for 1-2 weeks. Participants will get drugs and have blood and urine tests.
8. Participants will take an antibiotic and maybe an antiviral for at least 6 months after treatment. They will have repeat screening tests at visits every few months for the first year, every 6 months for the second year, then as determined.

This study will evaluate members in families with a history of small bowel carcinoid cancer to study the natural history of those family members that have the disease, determine ways to improve early detection by performing surveillance on those at risk but without disease and to identify the gene(s) that may cause the tumors. Familial carcinoid tumors usually originate in hormone-producing cells that line the small intestine or other cells of the digestive tract. The tumors are slow-growing and usually take many years before they cause symptoms. It is known that these tumors occur more often in some families and are then passed from one generation to the next by inherited genes.

Members of families, including all siblings and offspring in which two or more immediate blood relatives have had small bowel carcinoid tumors are eligible for this study. In some cases unaffected spouses of family members diagnosed with carcinoid cancer are also requested to participate by donating a sample of blood only.

Participants undergo a medical evaluation every 3 years during a 3- to 5-day hospital stay at the NIH Clinical Center. All participants have a personal and family medical history obtained and undergo a physical examination, blood and urine tests.

People who already have a small bowel carcinoid tumor or are at risk of developing a carcinoid tumor have some or all of the following procedures to determine the presence of carcinoid tumor and its (omit next two words- location or) spread to other areas of the body:

* Video Capsule Endoscopy: Visualization of the gastrointestinal tract by ingesting a disposable, "vitamin-pill sized" video capsule that has its own camera and light source.
* CT of the chest abdomen and pelvis with oral and IV contrast : X-ray examination of the chest, abdominal and pelvis organs.
* 18 FDOPA Positron emission tomography (PET) with CT for localization: Nuclear imaging scan to look at tumor activity.
* MRI Liver with contrast - to determine if disease has spread to liver
* Gallium 68 PET/CT-limited to individuals that have residual tumor.
* Clinical and research blood work

Background:

Small cell carcinoma of the bladder (SCCB) and other high-grade neuroendocrine tumors (HGNET) of the urinary tract are rare but aggressive cancers. Average survival for people diagnosed with SCCB or HGNET is about 1 year. Lurbinectedin and avelumab are drugs that are approved to treat other cancers. Researchers want to see if these drugs can help people with SCCB or HGNET.

Objective:

To test lurbinectedin with or without avelumab in people with SCCB or HGNET.
